user.title: Synology router or access point
user.description: Connect to one SRM device. Add each router and access point on its own; their client lists are combined. Help: [documentation]({docs})

data_description.host: Address or host name of the router or access point. With a certificate from a public authority (for example Let's Encrypt), its host name lets Home Assistant check the certificate by that name.
data_description.port: Leave empty for SRM's default: 8001 for HTTPS, 8000 for HTTP.
data_description.verify_certificate: Check the device's certificate: by the name it was issued for when a public authority vouches for it, else by its fingerprint after you confirmed it. Turn off only if you accept that anyone in your network could read the password.

certificate.title: Confirm the certificate
certificate.description:
The device presents a certificate with this SHA-256 fingerprint:

`{fingerprint}`

To compare it, open {url} in a browser, click the padlock or the warning next to the address and show the certificate; it lists the SHA-256 fingerprint. Continue only if both match; Home Assistant then trusts exactly this certificate. [How to compare]({docs})

certificate_public.title: Confirm the certificate
certificate_public.description:
The device presents a certificate issued by {issuer}, a public certificate authority, with this SHA-256 fingerprint:

`{fingerprint}`

**Check it by name (recommended):** enter the name the certificate was issued for, the one you open the device with in a browser (for example your DDNS name). Home Assistant then checks every connection against the authority and this name, and renewals need nothing from you.

**Pin it:** Leave the field empty, compare the fingerprint with the certificate shown at {url} in a browser and continue only if both match. Home Assistant then trusts exactly this certificate, and every renewal needs your confirmation. [More about certificates]({docs})

data_description.certificate_name: Only the name, for example router.example.net, without https:// and port. Home Assistant checks that the certificate is valid for it.

credentials.title: Administrator account
credentials.description: Use an SRM administrator account (only those are tested). Help: [documentation]({docs})

data_description.username: An SRM administrator account without two-factor authentication; a dedicated account is best.

clients.title: Device trackers
clients.description: Choose the clients Home Assistant should track. ● is online now, ○ is not; a date says when Home Assistant last saw the client. You can change this later in the options. [Help]({docs})

data_description.track_all: A tracker for every client that is online, has a name given in SRM, an IPv4 DHCP lease or reservation, or was seen in the last 30 days; new clients follow as they appear.
data_description.tracked: Only these clients get a tracker. Leave empty for none.
data_description.show_all: SRM keeps every client it ever saw. Turn on and continue to list them all, including ones gone long ago.
data_description.firewall_hits: A sensor that counts each rule's hits, for graphs and automations. The rule table on the Firewall rules sensor shows the hits either way.

reauth_confirm.title: Sign in again
reauth_confirm.description: Home Assistant could not sign in to {host}. Enter the account again.

data_description.username: An SRM administrator account without two-factor authentication; a dedicated account is best.

reauth_certificate.title: New certificate
reauth_certificate.description:
The device presents a certificate that does not match what Home Assistant trusted so far. Trusted so far: `{previous}` (a name stands for every valid certificate for that name, a fingerprint for exactly one certificate). If Home Assistant checked it by name so far, the certificate has probably expired or SRM is back to its own: renew it in SRM instead of pinning it here.

The certificate now presented:

`{fingerprint}`

This is expected after you renewed or replaced the certificate. Compare it with the certificate shown at {url} in a browser and continue only if both match; Home Assistant then trusts exactly this certificate. [How to compare]({docs})

reauth_certificate_public.description:

The certificate now presented is issued by {issuer}, a public certificate authority, with this SHA-256 fingerprint:

`{fingerprint}`

**Check it by name (recommended):** enter the name the certificate was issued for, the one you open the device with in a browser (for example your DDNS name). Home Assistant then checks every connection against the authority and this name, and renewals need nothing from you.

**Pin it:** Clear the field, compare the fingerprint with the certificate shown at {url} in a browser and continue only if both match. Home Assistant then trusts exactly this certificate, and every renewal needs your confirmation. [More about certificates]({docs})

reconfigure_unprotected.title: Stop checking the certificate?
reconfigure_unprotected.description: Home Assistant checks this device's certificate so far. Without the check, or over plain HTTP, anyone who can read traffic in your network could read the password, which is sent as soon as you continue. Continue only if you accept that; otherwise cancel. Help: [documentation]({docs})

Continue only if you accept that; otherwise cancel and set up the device again with HTTPS and a checked certificate. Use an SRM administrator account (only those are tested). blocked.title: {name} blocks Home Assistant
blocked.description: SRM's auto block refuses logins from Home Assistant after failed attempts, so {name} is not read. Home Assistant tries to log in again every 15 minutes; each attempt counts towards the block. Unblock Home Assistant's address in SRM's auto block settings, or wait until the block expires. This message disappears after the next successful update.

srm_from_internet.title: {name} allows access to SRM from the internet
srm_from_internet.description: SRM on {name} is set to allow access to its web interface from the internet. Wherever your connection lets it through, anyone who finds it can try to sign in, and a flaw in SRM would be open to the whole internet. Unless you need it while away, switch off the setting in SRM that allows access to SRM from the internet, and use a VPN instead. This message disappears once the setting is off.

auto_block_off.title: Auto block is off on {name}
auto_block_off.description: SRM's auto block is switched off on {name}, so nothing stops anyone from trying one password after another. Switch the auto block on in SRM. This message disappears once it is on.

firewall_open.title: The firewall of {name} lets the internet in
firewall_open.description: A default policy of the firewall on {name} allows traffic from the internet that no rule matches, to the router or to your network. Set the default policies for traffic from the internet to deny in SRM's firewall settings, and allow only what you need with rules. This message disappears once none of them allows.
